blocks.p: On the street below the humming building the August night was thick and wet, and the cicadas had not stopped since dusk. The last of the congregation went off in twos and threes toward the tram stop, fanning themselves with paper fans, talking about the heat and about what they would cook tomorrow. A man on a bicycle rode slowly past with a white lantern swinging from the handlebars. Across the road a vending machine glowed, full of cold tea and coffee in cans. Rei bought a can of barley tea, held it against his neck for a while, and then leaned against the shutter of the noodle shop.
He finally let himself draw the thing he had been refusing to draw all week. The wiring diagram. A diagram is colder than dread, and he needed something cold.

blocks.cap: Rei under the streetlight with Gin's book

blocks.p: He drew it on the back page of Gin's book, under the streetlight. Here was the city's grief, arriving the way it always had, a steady inheritance from the dead who were never properly sent home. Here was the Far-Shore Circle, gathering that grief into a battery and asking for nothing the bereaved were not desperate to give. And here were the two demons, drawing the battery down toward two opposite kinds of ruin. The Healer, the thing living in his brother, was thinning the Kita membrane gently. It wanted the dead let through cleanly, and the Thirteenth Seat filled with a quiet that Rei might almost mistake for kindness. And Kishin, through Rinka's kind mouth and Kaito's grieving one, was tearing at the same wall. It wanted the held breath to break all at once, and the muzzle to come off the dead forever. One wanted a door. The other wanted a wound. They were fighting over the same wall and feeding from the same room.
He turned back through the book to check a line, and a page he had flipped past a dozen times stopped him. Gin had drawn this diagram before. He had drawn it twice.

The page needed some knowing to read, and Rei knew just enough. Every practitioner's gift opened onto one of thirteen emotions, which the CVD called registers. Grief was one register, rage another, and so on round the wheel. For each register there was a seat, and someone or something held it. Gin's page was about who held them.

doc.title: Gin's page. The wheel, drawn twice
lines: The thirteen emotions sit twice. Picture two trees with the same thirteen fruit.

The first tree is the Thirteen as I have met them. Thirteen living mediums, each holding one register open and steady. Grief, rage, love, fear, wonder, despair, joy, shame, hunger, courage, longing, awe, duty. To the centre they are light anchors, clean points of pure register it feeds from to keep the membrane taut. A living holder, sane and willing, is the strongest thing in the world.

The second tree is the Qliphoth. Thirteen demon-shells of the same emotions. A Qliphoth does not make an emotion. It usurps an anchor. It eats the living holder out from under the seat and wears the register as a hollow shell. The seat still reads filled, but the light is gone and a hunger sits where a person stood.
So the war under everything is which tree holds the wheel. Light anchors can kill demons. Demons possess anchors.
VI. Despair. The holder is failing. Something on the dark side of the wheel is eating the seat out from under him.
XIII. Duty. Vacant since 2009. No living holder. The centre holds it directly from inside. Kita began to destabilise that year. After 2011 it went faster.
Only two shells on the dark tree have names I can find. The rest are loose across Tokyo and behind the veil. (G.U.)

blocks.p: Gin had left the names blank. Rei did not need him to fill them in. He wrote them himself, in pencil, next to his brother's ink. Beside VI, Despair, he wrote Kishin. Beside XIII, Duty, he held the pencil still for a long moment. Then he wrote Yushiro.
Underneath, smaller, Gin had added one more line in a different pen, as if he had come back to it on another night.

doc.title: Gin's later line, under the dark tree
lines: If one shell ever fed far enough, it would not want a seat. It would want the crown. The old books call the crown of the dark tree Thaumiel. A thing sitting there would be the inverse of whatever holds the centre now. Where the centre holds the membrane shut, it would tear it open and rule what pours through. A hell on this side, with a throne in it. (G.U.)

blocks.p: Rei read it twice. The old books Gin meant were the books of the Kabbalah, which drew the world as a tree, and the dark tree as its shadow. Thaumiel was the name they gave to the top of that shadow. Then Rei looked up at the third-floor windows, where the white paper glowed faintly over the noodle shop. He understood now what he had felt across the ring when Kishin let its appetite show. It meant to sit above all of them. Not only on the Despair seat it was already eating out from under its failing holder. Above the whole dark tree. Kishin was feeding to become the Inverted God, the dark mirror of the Axis. Every envelope in the lacquered box was a step toward that crown. If it got there, the two trees would stop being a drawing. The thirteen demons would move against the thirteen strongest mediums, and the city would be the ground they fought on.

And the Healer wanted it dead first. That was the other half of the drawing, and it was the half that made Rei's mouth go dry. The Healer did not want the crown. It wanted the Duty seat on the far side of the veil, the empty chair, so it could sit there beside the few of its own kind that it trusted. It did not want to rule the living. But it could not let Kishin rule them either. A demon can only be killed on this side from inside a body, Rinka had said, and his brother was the body. Gin was awake in there, watching it work.

A taxi went by with its light off. Somewhere above, an air conditioner dripped steadily onto the pavement. Rei had one more page of Gin's to use, and he used it the way Gin meant it to be used. It was a small card ruled in boxes, drawn for reading a group from the outside. Rei held it under the streetlight and went down it with his pencil.

doc.title: WARNING SIGNS field card. Reading a group from the outside
lines: [x] The comfort, luck or healing the group offers is real and reliable. Not vague faith, but something that demonstrably works. This is the tell, not the absence of one.
[x] A charismatic central figure who defers every question to the presence. Never claims authority personally. Always points past themselves to It.
[x] Rites that escalate in privacy. What newcomers see and what long members do have quietly diverged.
[x] Members who have given up money, time, secrets or outside relationships and describe the loss as growth.
[x] A before that no one will discuss. The originating event is sacred, fixed, and not to be examined.
[x] Veil residue at the meeting site that does not match the doctrine. The thing present is not the thing described.
[x] Members getting thinner, flatter, grief-heavier over months while insisting they have never been better. Watch the slope, not the snapshot.

blocks.p: Every box. He had not needed to think about any of them. The widow's sister. The lacquered box. The Touched who was with them in spirit. The cold shimmer that called itself the far shore. The two hollowed men under the photographs.

What stopped his breath on the dark street was the junction. In any honest wiring diagram there is one mark that matters, the place where the current could be cut. The answer was not the Healer, because he could not bring himself to cut Gin. The answer was not Kaito, because his sermon was built from true griefs, and making him a martyr would only fill the ring faster. The answer was the battery itself. The circle. Kanna-sensei and the thirty-five lightened faces. Cutting there meant giving every one of those people their grief back. It meant taking the peace away from the man from Sumida, and the widow, and the mother. It meant tearing comfort out of the bereaved to starve two catastrophes of the fuel they shared. The cleanest cut in the whole diagram ran straight through the most innocent room in it. Rei had read enough bodies to know that the cause of death is rarely where the cruelty is. The cruelty here was that mercy had been the supply line all along.

His phone had been warm in his pocket through the whole meeting. He took it out now and found what he knew he would find. There was a text from the unknown number that wrote in his brother's voice. It had been sent while he was drinking tea he should not have drunk.
You found the circle. Good. I was going to send you there next week.
Under it was a second message, and Rei could feel the pause before it even in the timestamp.
Don't cut the battery, Rei. I need it gentle. So do they.

It was the most reasonable thing the Healer had ever said to him, and it was asking him to leave the supply line running. And there was a worse part. On this one cold point, his brother's captor and his brother's mercy and his own exhausted heart all agreed, for the first time. That kept him standing very still against the shutter, while the cicadas sawed the dark to pieces.
